title: The incidence matrix: a hypergraph written as a table

what.formal: The incidence matrix of a hypergraph $H = (V, E)$ is the $|V| \times |E|$ matrix $H$ whose entry $H_{ve}$ is 1 if vertex $v$ belongs to hyperedge $e$ and 0 otherwise. Each row is a vertex and each column is one relation; the 1s in a column mark the members of that hyperedge.
what.plain: Make a table: one row per thing, one column per relation, and put a 1 wherever that thing takes part in that relation. That table is the hypergraph.

what.md: **Why this matrix, and not the adjacency matrix.** The adjacency matrix of card 1 stores *pairs*, so it cannot express a relation that holds five vertices at once without first inventing all ten pairs — which is exactly the information loss that motivated hypergraphs in the first place. The incidence matrix stores relations directly. It makes no assumption that a relation has two members, which is why the same object describes a plain graph (every column has two 1s) and a hypergraph (a column may have any number) without a change of notation.

Two conventions are worth fixing now, because this paper uses the second. Some authors index $H$ by edges first and vertices second; this paper writes it with **rows = vertices, columns = hyperedges**, and uses the letter $H$ for the matrix as well as the hypergraph. When you read Equation (3) later, $H_{ve}$ is the entry you have just built.

Note the collision of names: $H$ is both the hypergraph and its incidence matrix, and $E$ is both the edge set and (in Chapter 6's tables) an experimental setting. Papers reuse letters ruthlessly. Whenever a symbol appears, read what it is *doing* in that line rather than trusting the letter.

example.md: **Example 1 — the dorm, as a table.** Three students, one relation. Rows: Zhang, Li, Wang. Columns: the single hyperedge "dorm 302".

example.note: Three rows, one column, all three entries 1 — every student takes part in the one relation. This is the smallest possible hypergraph that is **not** a plain graph, because its single column has three 1s rather than two.

gloss.md: the incidence matrix — rows are vertices, columns are hyperedges
1 exactly when vertex $v$ is a member of hyperedge $e$

example.md: **Example 2 — the same table for a plain graph.** Take the four-person graph again, with rows 1–4 and columns $e_1=\{1,2\}$, $e_2=\{2,3\}$, $e_3=\{2,4\}$:

example.note: Read column $e_2$: the 1s sit in rows 2 and 3, so $e_2 = \{2,3\}$. **A column tells you its own members** — you never need the drawing again.

gloss.md: vertex 2 is in edge $e_2$, so this entry is 1
vertex 1 is not in edge $e_2$, so this entry is 0

example.md: Compare the two matrices above and you have the whole difference between the two kinds of object: in the dorm's incidence matrix one column holds three 1s; in the graph's every column holds exactly two. **A plain graph is precisely the case where every column has exactly two 1s** — the same statement the title-decode card made about hyperedges, now visible in the arithmetic.

quiz.q: In this paper's convention, what does a column of the incidence matrix represent?

opts.md: One vertex and the relations it belongs to
opts.expl: That is a row. Rows and columns are transposes of each other, so mixing them up is easy and consequential — it silently swaps the two degree columns of Table I.

opts.md: One hyperedge, with 1s marking its members
opts.expl: Correct. A column is a relation; the 1s in it name the vertices that take part. This is what makes the incidence matrix able to describe a relation of any size.
The count of hyperedges is the *number* of columns, not the content of any one of them.

quiz.q: A hypergraph has 7 vertices and 4 hyperedges. How many entries does its incidence matrix have in total?
quiz.hint: The matrix has one row per vertex and one column per hyperedge.
quiz.sol: The matrix is $7 \times 4$, so it has $7 \times 4 = 28$ entries. The number of 1s inside it is a different quantity — that is the total membership count, which you would need the actual edges to know.

quiz.q: Why does this paper write its network layer in terms of the incidence matrix rather than the adjacency matrix?

opts.md: Because the incidence matrix is smaller
opts.expl: It is usually *larger*: $|V| \times |E|$ entries against $|V| \times |V|$ for adjacency, and $|E|$ can be comparable to $|V|$.

opts.md: Because it can express relations among any number of vertices, which is what the data actually contains
opts.expl: Correct. Converting a co-authorship hyperedge of 982 authors into an adjacency matrix would require up to 481,671 entries for that one relation — and once expanded, no operation could tell that those pairs came from a single event. The incidence matrix keeps relations intact, which is exactly what Equation (3) needs in order to count them.

opts.md: Because adjacency matrices cannot be used with neural networks
opts.expl: They can — ordinary graph neural networks use adjacency-like operators routinely. The reason here is expressiveness about group relations, not a limitation of the tool.

close: **Where this is going:** the incidence matrix is the object in the paper's Equation (3), where each vertex's membership count is summed over hyperedges. Card 4 does that sum and shows it is the vertex degree.
